plain_english: We should also stay flexible and not get too attached to whatever life fate has given us. When chance leads us somewhere new, we should go with it. Don't fear changes to your plans or your place in life. Just don't let yourself become fickle — that's the worst enemy of peace of mind. Stubbornness makes you anxious and miserable, especially when Fortune forces you to give in anyway. But fickleness is even worse, since it can never settle down. Both extremes — never changing anything and being unhappy with everything — are enemies of inner peace. Your mind should turn away from focusing on outside things and focus on itself instead. Let it trust itself, enjoy itself, and admire its own work. Avoid other people's affairs as much as possible and devote yourself to yourself. Don't feel every loss so deeply, and try to see even misfortunes in a good light.
original_excerpt: Moreover, we ought to cultivate an easy temper, and not become over fond of the lot which fate has assigned to us, but transfer ourselves to whatever other condition chance may lead us to, and fear no alteration, either in our purposes or our position in life, provided that we do not become subject to caprice, which of all vices is the most hostile to repose: for obstinacy, from which Fortune often wrings some concession, must needs be anxious and unhappy, but caprice, which can never restrain itself, must be more so. Both of these qualities, both that of altering nothing, and that of being dissatisfied with everything, are energies to repose. The mind ought in all cases to be called away from the contemplation of external things to that of itself: let it confide in itself, rejoice in itself, admire its own works; avoid as far as may be those of others, and devote itself to itself; let it not feel losses, and put a good construction even upon misfortunes.

plain_english: Zeno, the founder of our school, heard that his ship had sunk and all his wealth was gone. He said, "Fortune is telling me to pursue philosophy with less baggage." A tyrant threatened Theodorus with death and told him he wouldn't even get a proper burial. Theodorus replied, "Do whatever makes you happy. You can spill my blood if you want. But burial? You'd have to be an idiot to think I care whether I rot above ground or below it."
original_excerpt: Zeno, the chief of our school, when he heard the news of a shipwreck, in which all his property had been lost, remarked, "Fortune bids me follow philosophy in lighter marching order." A tyrant threatened Theodorus with death, and even with want of burial. "You are able to please yourself," he answered, "my half pint of blood is in your power: for, as for burial, what a fool you must be if you suppose that I care whether I rot above ground or under it."

plain_english: Julius Kanus was an extraordinary man. Even being born in our wicked century doesn't stop us from admiring him. He had a long argument with Gaius. As Kanus was leaving, that tyrant said to him, "Don't fool yourself with false hopes. I've ordered your execution." Kanus replied, "Thank you, most excellent prince." I'm not sure what he meant. Several explanations come to mind. Was he being sarcastic to show Gaius how cruel he was — making death seem like a gift? Was he mocking Gaius's usual madness? After all, even people whose children were killed and property seized used to thank him. Or did Kanus genuinely welcome death as freedom? Whatever he meant, it was a brave answer. Someone might say, "After this, Gaius could have spared him." Kanus wasn't worried about that. Everyone knew Gaius always followed through on execution orders.
original_excerpt: Julius Kanus, a man of peculiar greatness, whom even the fact of his having been born in this century does not prevent our admiring, had a long dispute with Gaius, and when as he was going away that Phalaris of a man said to him, "That you may not delude yourself with any foolish hopes, I have ordered you to be executed," he answered, "I thank you, most excellent prince." I am not sure what he meant: for many ways of explaining his conduct occur to me. Did he wish to be reproachful, and to show him how great his cruelty must be if death became a kindness? or did he upbraid him with his accustomed insanity? for even those whose children were put to death, and whose goods were confiscated, used to thank him: or was it that he willingly received death, regarding it as freedom? Whatever he meant, it was a magnanimous answer. Some one may say, "After this Gaius might have let him live." Kanus had no fear of this: the good faith with which Gaius carried out such orders as these was well known.

plain_english: Can you believe this man spent his last ten days without any despair? It's amazing how he spoke and acted. How calm he was. He was playing checkers when the centurion came to collect the men scheduled for execution. When called, he counted his pieces and told his opponent, "Don't lie after I'm dead and claim you were winning." Then he turned to the centurion and said, "You can confirm I'm ahead by one piece." Do you think Kanus was just playing a game? No — he was making a point about life itself. His friends were sad they were losing such a great man. "Why are you upset?" he asked. "You wonder if our souls live on after death. Well, I'm about to find out."
original_excerpt: Will you believe that he passed the ten intervening days before his execution without the slightest despondency? it is marvellous how that man spoke and acted, and how peaceful he was. He was playing at draughts when the centurion in charge of a number of those who where going to be executed bade him join them: on the summons he counted his men and said to his companion, "Mind you do not tell a lie after my death, and say that you won;" then, turning to the centurion, he said "You will bear me witness that I am one man ahead of him." Do you think that Kanus played upon that draught-board? nay, he played with it. His friends were sad at being about to lose so great a man: "Why," asked he, "are you sorrowful? you are enquiring whether our souls are immortal, but I shall presently know."

plain_english: Right up until the end, he never stopped searching for truth. He even debated questions about his own death. His philosophy teacher walked with him, and they were close to the hill where the daily sacrifice to Caesar our god was made. His teacher asked, "What are you thinking about right now, Kanus? What's on your mind?" "I've decided," Kanus answered, "to watch very carefully in that quickest moment of all — to see if my spirit will know it's leaving my body." He even promised that if he learned anything, he would visit his friends and tell them what it's like for souls after death. Here was calm right in the middle of a storm. Here was a soul that deserved eternal life — one that used his own fate to test the truth. At life's final step, he experimented with his own dying breath. He didn't just keep learning until he died. He learned something even from death itself. No one has taken the philosopher's life further than this. I won't rush past this great man who deserves our respect. I will pass you down to all future generations, you most noble heart, the greatest among all of Gaius's many victims.
original_excerpt: Nor did he up to the very end cease his search after truth, and raised arguments upon the subject of his own death. His own teacher of philosophy accompanied him, and they were not far from the hill on which the daily sacrifice to Caesar our god was offered, when he said, "What are you thinking of now, Kanus? or what are your ideas?" "I have decided," answered Kanus, "at that most swiftly-passing moment of all to watch whether the spirit will be conscious of the act of leaving the body." He promised, too, that if he made any discoveries, he would come round to his friends and tell them what the condition of the souls of the departed might be. Here was peace in the very midst of the storm: here was a soul worthy of eternal life, which used its own fate as a proof of truth, which when at the last step of life experimented upon his fleeting breath, and did not merely continue to learn until he died, but learned something even from death itself. No man has carried the life of a philosopher further. I will not hastily leave the subject of a great man, and one who deserves to be spoken of with respect: I will hand thee down to all posterity, thou most noble heart, chief among the many victims of Gaius.
